scenes.title: Find both axis crossings
body: What must be zero on each axis?
scenes.narration: Suppose you have three x plus two y equals twelve, and the question asks for both intercepts. Here’s the idea: intercepts are not two unrelated formulas. They are the two places where the same line meets the coordinate axes, and each axis forces one coordinate to be zero.

scenes.title: The axes tell you what to set to zero
body: Common mistake: setting x = 0 for the x-intercept
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. For the x-intercept, you do not set x equal to zero. A point on the x-axis has y equal to zero, so the x-intercept has the form x comma zero. On the y-axis, x equals zero, so the y-intercept has the form zero comma y.

scenes.title: Find the x-intercept
scenes.narration: First restrict the equation to the x-axis by replacing y with zero. Three x plus two times zero equals twelve, so three x equals twelve and x equals four. The x-intercept is the point four comma zero. Notice why this works: we are finding the point that satisfies both the line equation and the condition for being on the x-axis.

scenes.title: Find the y-intercept
scenes.narration: Now use the same equation again, but restrict it to the y-axis. Set x equal to zero. Then two y equals twelve, so y equals six. The y-intercept is zero comma six. The important idea is that you are not switching formulas; you are changing which axis condition you impose on the same line.

scenes.title: Check both points
scenes.narration: Quick check: four comma zero gives twelve, and zero comma six also gives twelve, so both points lie on the line. Recap the idea: the x-axis forces y to zero, the y-axis forces x to zero, and those two conditions reveal the two intercepts. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
